topics.title: What is a Database?
topics.content:

What is a Database?

Beginner ⏱️ 5 min read

A database is an organized collection of structured information, or data, typically stored electronically in a computer system. A database is usually controlled by a database management system (DBMS).

Key Concepts

  • Data: Facts and statistics collected together for reference or analysis.
  • Table: A collection of related data held in a structured format within a database. It consists of columns and rows.
  • Row (Record): A single, implicitly structured data item in a table.
  • Column (Field): A set of data values of a particular simple type, one value for each row of the database.

topics.content:

Database Management Systems (DBMS)

Beginner ⏱️ 6 min read

A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that interacts with end-users, applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze the data. The DBMS software additionally encompasses the core facilities provided to administer the database.

RDBMS (Relational DBMS)

An RDBMS is a type of DBMS that stores data in a row-based table structure which connects related data elements. RDBMS includes functions that maintain the security, accuracy, integrity, and consistency of the data. SQL is the standard language used to interact with an RDBMS.

Popular RDBMS Examples

  • MySQL
  • PostgreSQL
  • Oracle Database
  • Microsoft SQL Server
  • SQLite

topics.content:

Types of SQL Commands

Core Concept ⏱️ 8 min read

SQL commands are instructions used to communicate with the database. They are broadly categorized into four types:

1. DDL (Data Definition Language)

Used to define the database structure or schema.

  • CREATE: Creates a new table, database, schema, etc.
  • ALTER: Modifies an existing database object.
  • DROP: Deletes an entire table, view of a table, or other objects in the database.
  • TRUNCATE: Removes all records from a table, but not its structure.

2. DML (Data Manipulation Language)

Used for managing data within schema objects.

  • SELECT: Retrieves data from the database.
  • INSERT: Inserts data into a table.
  • UPDATE: Updates existing data within a table.
  • DELETE: Deletes records from a table.

3. DCL (Data Control Language)

Used to control access to data in the database.

  • GRANT: Gives user access privileges to database.
  • REVOKE: Withdraws user access privileges.

4. TCL (Transaction Control Language)

Used to manage transactions in the database.

  • COMMIT: Commits a transaction.
  • ROLLBACK: Rollbacks a transaction in case of any error occurs.
  • SAVEPOINT: Sets a savepoint within a transaction.

topics.content:

Basic SQL Queries

Essential ⏱️ 15 min read

SQL queries allow you to manage databases, create tables, and manipulate data (retrieve, insert, update, and delete).

Create and Drop Databases

Before doing anything with data, you must first create a database using CREATE DATABASE. To delete it, use DROP DATABASE.

Database Queries Syntax
CREATE DATABASE databasename;
DROP DATABASE databasename;

The CREATE TABLE Statement

The CREATE TABLE statement is used to create a new table in a database. You must specify the name of the table and the columns (along with their data types).

CREATE TABLE Syntax
CREATE TABLE Users (
    ID int,
    Name varchar(255),
    Age int
);

The SELECT Statement

The SELECT statement is used to select data from a database. The data returned is stored in a result table, called the result-set.

SELECT Syntax
SELECT column1, column2 FROM table_name;

The WHERE Clause

The WHERE clause is used to filter records. It is used to extract only those records that fulfill a specified condition.

WHERE Syntax
SELECT * FROM table_name WHERE condition;

INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE

These commands are used to modify data in the tables.

-- Insert a new record
INSERT INTO Users (Name, Age) VALUES ('Alice', 30);

-- Update an existing record
UPDATE Users SET Age = 31 WHERE Name = 'Alice';

-- Delete a record
DELETE FROM Users WHERE Name = 'Alice';

topics.title: SQL Constraints
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > SQL > SQL

SQL Constraints

Core Concept ⏱️ 10 min read

What are Constraints?

Constraints are rules applied to table columns to ensure the accuracy, consistency, and integrity of the data stored in a database. In simple words, constraints prevent invalid data from being inserted into the database.

Why do we use Constraints?

Imagine a student database. Every student should have a unique ID, student name should not be empty, email should not be duplicated, admission date should have today's date if not provided, and student ID should automatically increase. All these rules are implemented using constraints.

Types of Constraints

1. PRIMARY KEY

A PRIMARY KEY is a column (or combination of columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table. Values must be unique, cannot contain NULL, and only one PRIMARY KEY is allowed per table.

PRIMARY KEY Example
CREATE TABLE Student(
    student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    student_name VARCHAR(100)
);

2. NOT NULL

The NOT NULL constraint ensures that a column must always contain a value. It prevents empty values.

NOT NULL Example
CREATE TABLE Employee(
    id INT,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

3. UNIQUE

The UNIQUE constraint ensures that all values in a column are different. Duplicate values are not allowed. Unlike PRIMARY KEY, a table can have multiple UNIQUE constraints (e.g., Email, Aadhaar Number, Passport Number).

PRIMARY KEY UNIQUE
Only one per table Many allowed
Cannot be NULL Can contain NULL
Uniquely identifies each row Ensures unique values
Automatically indexed Automatically indexed

4. DEFAULT

The DEFAULT constraint automatically assigns a value if the user does not provide one during insertion.

DEFAULT Example
CREATE TABLE Employee(
    id INT,
    salary DECIMAL(10,2) DEFAULT 15000
);

5. AUTO_INCREMENT

AUTO_INCREMENT automatically generates sequential numbers whenever a new record is inserted. No need to manually enter IDs.

AUTO_INCREMENT Example
CREATE TABLE Student(
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100)
);

INSERT INTO Student(name)
VALUES ('Mohamed'), ('Rahul'), ('Priya');

topics.title: Primary Key
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > SQL > SQL

Primary Key

Essential ⏱️ 6 min read

The PRIMARY KEY constraint uniquely identifies each record in a table.

Characteristics of a Primary Key

  • Primary keys must contain UNIQUE values.
  • A primary key column cannot contain NULL values.
  • A table can have only ONE primary key.
  • The primary key can consist of single or multiple columns (composite key).
Creating a Primary Key
CREATE TABLE Persons (
    ID int NOT NULL,
    LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL,
    FirstName varchar(255),
    Age int,
    PRIMARY KEY (ID)
);

topics.title: Unique Key
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > SQL > SQL

Unique Key

Essential ⏱️ 5 min read

The UNIQUE constraint ensures that all values in a column are different.

UNIQUE vs PRIMARY KEY

Both the UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY constraints provide a guarantee for uniqueness for a column or set of columns.

A PRIMARY KEY constraint automatically has a UNIQUE constraint. However, you can have many UNIQUE constraints per table, but only one PRIMARY KEY constraint per table.

Creating a Unique Key
CREATE TABLE Persons (
    ID int NOT NULL,
    LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL,
    FirstName varchar(255),
    Age int,
    UNIQUE (ID)
);

topics.content:

SQL Data Types

Core Concept ⏱️ 15 min read

What is a Data Type?

A Data Type defines the type of value that can be stored in a table column. It tells MySQL what kind of data can be stored, how much storage space is required, and what operations can be performed on the data.

Example Table with Data Types
CREATE TABLE Student(
    id INT,
    name VARCHAR(100),
    age INT,
    fees DECIMAL(10,2),
    dob DATE
);

Categories of Data Types in MySQL

MySQL data types are divided into 5 categories:

1. Numeric Data Types

Used to store numbers. Divided into Integer Types and Decimal/Floating Point Types.

Data Type Storage Example Usage
TINYINT1 ByteAge
SMALLINT2 BytesMarks
MEDIUMINT3 BytesPopulation
INT4 BytesStudent ID
BIGINT8 BytesLarge IDs

Decimal Types:

  • FLOAT: Approximate decimal values. Used for height, weight, scientific calculations. May lose precision.
  • DOUBLE: More accurate than FLOAT. Suitable for GPS coordinates, large decimal calculations.
  • DECIMAL: Stores exact decimal values (e.g., DECIMAL(10,2) means 10 digits total, 2 after decimal).

2. String (Character) Data Types

Used to store text.

  • CHAR: Fixed-length string. Suitable for Gender, Country Code, Blood Group.
  • VARCHAR: Variable-length string. Suitable for Name, Address, Email.
  • TEXT: Stores very large text. Suitable for Feedback, Comments, Articles.

3. Date and Time Data Types

Used to store date and time.

Data Type Stores
DATEDate only
TIMETime only
DATETIMEDate + Time
TIMESTAMPDate + Time (often auto-managed)
YEARYear only

4. Boolean Data Type

MySQL treats BOOLEAN as an alias for TINYINT(1).

5. Binary Data Types

Used to store binary data such as images, files, or encrypted content.

  • BINARY: Fixed-length binary data.
  • VARBINARY: Variable-length binary data (e.g., password hash).
  • BLOB: Stores large binary data like images, PDFs, audio, video.

Complete Example

Comprehensive Table Creation
CREATE TABLE Employee(
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100),
    age TINYINT,
    salary DECIMAL(10,2),
    email VARCHAR(100),
    gender CHAR(1),
    department ENUM('HR','IT','Sales'),
    skills SET('Java','Python','React','SQL'),
    joining_date DATE,
    login_time TIME,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    isActive BOOLEAN,
    profile_photo BLOB
);
